title: The Verge and the Grave: Poe from the Boston Stage to Westminster Hall
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Boston, the birth into the theatre trade
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Two traveling actors, David Poe Jr. and Eliza Arnold Hopkins Poe, are working the Boston stage when their second son is born on the nineteenth of January. The theatre is the family trade and the family address; the boy's first year is measured in engagements and rented rooms. Within a year the father is gone from the household and out of the record. Within two the mother is dead of pulmonary tuberculosis, twenty-four years old. The city gets him for less than a year of infancy and will wait two centuries to put up a statue of him walking back in.
suggested_refs: The Boston theatre circuit of 1808-1809, where David and Eliza Poe were under engagement

stops.name: Richmond, the mother dies and the Allans take him in
stops.date_confidence: year attested (1811); the verified pool gives no month or day, and December is the month recorded for Eliza Poe's death in the standard chronologies, not in the pool itself
stops.campa: Eliza Poe dies of pulmonary tuberculosis at Richmond and the three orphaned children are separated. Edgar is taken into the house of John Allan, a Scottish tobacco merchant, and his wife Frances, who wants the boy and gets him. He is baptized into the Episcopal Church the following year and given the middle name he will carry the rest of his life. He is never legally adopted and never made an heir. The arrangement is affection on one side of the house and account-keeping on the other, and it holds for as long as the accounts do.
suggested_refs: The Allan house and counting room in Richmond, Virginia, 1811-1815

stops.name: Chelsea, the school of the Misses Dubourg
stops.date_confidence: the pool's single 1815 entry welds together two schools; eapoe.org places Poe at the Dubourg school under 1816 and Wikipedia says he studied there until summer 1817, so the Irvine grammar school is 1815-16 and Chelsea 1816-17. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January
stops.campa: The Allans sail for the United Kingdom in 1815 and the boy is put through the schools of two countries. First a grammar school at Irvine in Ayrshire, John Allan's own home ground, then a boarding school in Chelsea kept by the Misses Dubourg at 146 Sloane Street. He is seven, then eight, an American child learning to recite in an English classroom and to answer to a name that is only half his. The Dubourg surname will surface twenty-five years later in the Rue Morgue, fastened to a laundress who heard voices through a door.
suggested_refs: 146 Sloane Street, Chelsea, the boarding school of the Misses Dubourg

stops.name: Stoke Newington, the Manor House School
stops.date_confidence: sources differ: Wikipedia implies 1817, the eapoe.org Poe Chronology dates the entry under 1818. Not resolved here. Month and day unknown, defaulted to January
stops.campa: Four miles north of London, at Stoke Newington, the Reverend John Bransby keeps the Manor House School, and Poe is entered there for the last stretch of the English years. The village is brick and elm at the edge of the market gardens. The school stands behind a wall, a rambling house kept by a clergyman with a living to hold and boys to birch. The pupil will lift the master's name whole for the double in William Wilson and build the school around it from memory. Whether he arrives in 1817 or in 1818, the sources will not agree.
suggested_refs: The Manor House School of the Reverend John Bransby, Stoke Newington, then four miles outside London

stops.name: Richmond, the return and the Galt fortune
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day not given in the pool, defaulted to January
stops.campa: The Allans come back to Richmond in 1820 and the boy resumes an American boyhood on Virginia money. At fifteen he serves as a lieutenant of a Richmond youth honor guard turned out for the city. In 1825 John Allan's uncle William Galt dies and leaves an estate large enough to change the family's standing overnight; Allan buys Moldavia, a house with a ballroom, and moves his household into it. Poe grows up inside a fortune that will never be written in his direction, courting a neighbor's daughter, Sarah Elmira Royster.
suggested_refs: Moldavia, the Richmond house bought by John Allan out of the Galt estate, 1825

segments.name: The Rupture and the Assumed Name

stops.name: Charlottesville, ten months at the University
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He registers at Jefferson's new university on the fourteenth of February to read ancient and modern languages, and he is good at it. John Allan sends him with less money than the session costs. Poe covers the gap at cards and loses, and the debts run past anything his foster father will touch. He learns that Elmira Royster is engaged to another man, her father having intercepted what he wrote her. In December he leaves after a single session, ten months rather than the year the histories usually grant him, and the quarrel with Allan is permanent.
suggested_refs: Room 13, West Range, University of Virginia, kept as Poe's room

stops.name: Boston, Tamerlane and Other Poems, by a Bostonian
stops.date_confidence: year attested only; the pool gives 1827 without month for the book, and April 1827 for the arrival in Boston. Month and day defaulted to January, so this stop sits before the May enlistment in sequence though the book itself was printed later in the year
stops.campa: Eighteen years old and out of the Allan house, he goes back to the city he was born in and lives on odd jobs he does not name afterward. There he finds a printer willing to set forty pages of verse, and the book appears with no author on it, only the words By a Bostonian. About fifty copies are run off. It is reviewed by nobody and sold to almost nobody. A handful of copies survive into the next century and become among the most valuable books ever printed in America. In his own lifetime the book earns him nothing and no second edition of it is called for.
suggested_refs: Tamerlane and Other Poems (Boston, 1827), the anonymous first book

stops.name: Fort Independence, the enlistment of Edgar A. Perry
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of May, four months after his eighteenth birthday, he signs on for five years in the United States Army as Edgar A. Perry, clerk, aged twenty-two. Both the name and the age are false and the Army does not check. He is posted to Fort Independence on Castle Island in Boston Harbor, a granite star set in the water within sight of the streets he was born among. He turns out to be a good soldier: punctual, sober, quick at the paperwork, and promoted.
suggested_refs: Fort Independence, Castle Island, Boston Harbor, first post of Private Edgar A. Perry

stops.name: Fort Moultrie, the brig Waltham and the Carolina sand
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the eighth of November the company embarks on the brig Waltham for Charleston, and Poe spends the following year on Sullivan's Island at Fort Moultrie, sand and palmetto and the Atlantic on three sides. He is set to work as an artificer, preparing shells and cartridges, which is exacting labor for a man of nineteen. The island goes into the fiction later and stays there: the treasure of The Gold-Bug comes out of this sand, and the scarab and the cipher and the ruined mansion are furnished from these dunes.
suggested_refs: Fort Moultrie, Sullivan's Island, South Carolina, and the sand of 'The Gold-Bug'

stops.name: Fort Monroe, the sergeant major buys his way out
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Transferred north to Fort Monroe at Old Point Comfort, he rises through the artillery to sergeant major, the highest rank a non-commissioned soldier can hold, inside two years of service. Then he wants out, and out requires a substitute enlistee and money. Frances Allan dies at Richmond on the twenty-eighth of February; the grief buys a truce with John Allan long enough to get the arrangement made. On the fifteenth of April he is discharged, replacement found and paid, and turns toward West Point with a soldier's record and no prospects.
suggested_refs: Fort Monroe, Old Point Comfort, Virginia, where Poe served as sergeant major of artillery

segments.name: Baltimore, West Point, and the Third Book

stops.name: Baltimore, the house of Maria Clemm and Al Aaraaf
stops.date_confidence: the Baltimore move is dated 1829 without a month in the pool; John Neal's notice is September 1829 and the book December 1829 per eapoe.org, so the stop is dated to the book
stops.campa: He goes to Baltimore, to the crowded house of his widowed aunt Maria Clemm: her daughter Virginia, seven years old, his brother Henry, and his grandmother Elizabeth Cairnes Poe, whose widow's pension is holding the household up. In September the critic John Neal prints an encouraging notice of verses Poe has sent him, the first praise from anyone in the trade. In December, Hatch and Dunning of Baltimore publish Al Aaraaf, Tamerlane and Minor Poems with his name on the title page. This is the family he will keep.
suggested_refs: Al Aaraaf, Tamerlane and Minor Poems (Baltimore: Hatch & Dunning, December 1829)

stops.name: West Point, the cadet
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the first of July he matriculates at the United States Military Academy, older than his classmates and already twice a published poet, which he does not conceal. He is strong in French and in mathematics. In October John Allan marries Louisa Patterson, his second wife, and there will be legitimate heirs; whatever remained of Poe's expectation of Richmond money closes that month. He is on the plateau above the Hudson drilling toward a commission on a plan that has just lost the whole of its point.
suggested_refs: The United States Military Academy register of cadets, class entering July 1830

stops.name: West Point, the court-martial he arranged
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Unable to resign without a guardian's consent that Allan will not give, he takes the other exit: he stops going. He misses formations, then classes, then the orders that follow from missing them, and he builds the record up deliberately until the Academy has no choice left. On the eighth of February he is tried for gross neglect of duty and disobedience of orders, pleads in the way that guarantees conviction, and is dismissed. It is the second institution he has left by making himself impossible to keep, and the last one that will ever take him in.
suggested_refs: The West Point court-martial proceedings of 8 February 1831 against Cadet E. A. Poe

stops.name: New York, the third volume
stops.date_confidence: the pool gives February 1831 without a day, defaulted to the first; the volume itself was printed after the 8 February court-martial, so the stop is out of strict sequence with the previous one
stops.campa: He goes down the Hudson to New York carrying a subscription list: the cadets have each put in a dollar and a quarter toward a book of poems by the man they watched engineer his own expulsion. Elam Bliss prints it and Poe dedicates it to the corps. The cadets, expecting more of the satirical verses he had circulated about their officers, receive Israfel and To Helen and a preface lecturing them on the nature of poetry. By March he is back in Baltimore with no money and a third book nobody wants.
suggested_refs: Poems by Edgar A. Poe, Second Edition (New York: Elam Bliss, 1831), dedicated to the U.S. Corps of Cadets

stops.name: Baltimore, the brother dies and the prize is won
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death; the Amity Street residence and the Saturday Visiter prize fall in 1833 and are carried in the campa of this stop
stops.campa: On the first of August his elder brother William Henry Leonard Poe dies in the Clemm house, twenty-four years old, of complications the family attributes to drink. Poe stays on. The household settles at 203 North Amity Street and lives on Maria Clemm's scraping, and he turns from verse to prose because prose sells. In 1833 the Baltimore Saturday Visiter gives him its prize for MS. Found in a Bottle, a story about a ship carried south on a current toward the pole and swallowed at the end of it.
suggested_refs: 203 North Amity Street, Baltimore, the Clemm household of the early 1830s
sources: Wikipedia, 'Edgar Allan Poe House and Museum'

segments.name: The Verge: the Doctrine Before Pym

stops.name: London, the nested shells of Edmond Halley
stops.date_confidence: the 1692 proposal is attested; month and day defaulted to January. This stop is a genealogy pin, not an event in Poe's life
stops.campa: Before the Royal Society, Edmond Halley proposes that the Earth is not solid: an outer shell some five hundred miles thick with three concentric spheres turning inside it at rates of their own, each possibly lit and possibly inhabited, the whole of it accounting for why the compass wanders. It is a real proposal by a real astronomer and it stays in the literature. A folk genealogy will later hang Athanasius Kircher and Leonard Euler on the same line, wrongly in Euler's case, and hand the lineage forward to Poe.
suggested_refs: Halley's 1692 paper on the variation of the compass and the concentric shells
sources: Edward Sandifer, 'Euler and the Hollow Earth' (2007), on the misattribution

stops.name: St. Louis, Circular No. 1
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: John Cleves Symmes Jr., infantry captain retired to trade on the upper Mississippi, prints a broadside and mails five hundred copies of it to every learned society, college and legislature he can name. The Earth is hollow, habitable within, open at the poles. He pledges his life to proving it and asks for one hundred brave companions. He names three protectors without asking them first: Alexander von Humboldt, Humphry Davy, Samuel Mitchill. The sheet is dated the tenth of April and none of the three ever answers it.
stops.quote: I declare the earth is hollow, and habitable within; containing a number of solid concentrick spheres, one within the other, and that it is open at the poles 12 or 16 degrees; I pledge my life in support of this truth, and am ready to explore the hollow, if the world will support and aid me in the undertaking.
stops.quote_source: John Cleves Symmes, Circular No. 1, St. Louis, Missouri Territory, April 10, 1818
suggested_refs: Surviving copies of Symmes's Circular No. 1, with the attached certificate of sanity

stops.name: Paris, the naturalist says nothing
stops.date_confidence: the arrival of the Circular in Paris is dated 1818-09-01 in humboldt.journey.json; day and month there are themselves a reconstruction
stops.campa: The broadside crosses the Atlantic and reaches Alexander von Humboldt at his Paris desk, where he is deep into the thirty volumes of the Voyage aux regions equinoxiales and decades away from beginning Kosmos. He is being appointed, without consultation, protector of a theory of concentric habitable spheres by an American captain he has never met. He answers with silence, total and permanent. It is the same desk at which Bolivar found him in 1804, in the city where Marie Bonaparte will later keep house for Freud.
suggested_refs: Humboldt's Paris desk, the shared pin of humboldt.journey.json, bolivar.journey.json and freud.journey.json

stops.name: Cincinnati, the wooden globe
stops.date_confidence: the pool and symmes.journey.json both date the first Cincinnati lectures to 1820 without month or day; defaulted to January
stops.campa: Symmes carries the doctrine into the lecture halls of the Ohio valley with a wooden model in his hands: a globe cut open at both ends, sphere inside sphere, the polar verges rimmed so gradually that a ship could sail over one without knowing it had crossed. Warm seas lie within, lit by refracted light, and he offers the migrations of birds and whales as the proof of them. The newspapers call him the Newton of the West and a lunatic in the same column. Eighteen years later this is the machinery under the last chapter of Pym.
suggested_refs: Symmes's sectioned wooden globe, exhibited on the Ohio and Kentucky lecture circuit

stops.name: Hamilton, Ohio, the hollow globe over the grave
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death; the monument was raised by Americus Symmes afterward, date not given in the pool
stops.campa: Symmes dies at Hamilton on the twenty-ninth of May, six months short of forty-nine, worn out by lecture tours and unshaken to the end. Congress has tabled his petitions twice. His son Americus raises a stone over the grave and sets on it a globe of freestone cut hollow and open at both poles, the only monument the theory has ever received anywhere. It stands in a small park in Ohio. Nine years after the burial a bankrupt magazine writer in Philadelphia sends a fictional ship through the opening it represents.
stops.quote: The Earth is hollow, habitable within, and widely open about the poles.
stops.quote_source: Americus Symmes, Symmes's Theory of Concentric Spheres (1878), title compiled from his father's writings
suggested_refs: The Symmes monument, Hamilton, Ohio, with its hollow freestone globe

segments.name: The Messenger, the Cousin, and the Polar Book

stops.name: Richmond, the Messenger and the wedding at the boarding house
stops.date_confidence: attested for the wedding; the Messenger appointment (1835, month not given) and the Baltimore marriage licence (22 September 1835) are carried in the campa of this stop
stops.campa: The Southern Literary Messenger takes him on as assistant editor in 1835, discharges him within weeks, and takes him back. He reviews American books with a hatchet and the subscription list climbs. On the twenty-second of September 1835 he obtains a licence in Baltimore to marry his first cousin Virginia Clemm, thirteen years old; he is twenty-six. On the sixteenth of May 1836 a Presbyterian minister marries them in a Richmond boarding house, Maria Clemm standing by, Virginia given out as twenty-one.
suggested_refs: The Baltimore marriage licence of 22 September 1835 and the Richmond ceremony of 16 May 1836

stops.name: Richmond, the review of Reynolds's Address
stops.date_confidence: January 1837 attested for both the review and the departure from the Messenger; day not given, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: In the January Messenger he reviews Jeremiah N. Reynolds's Address on the Subject of a Surveying and Exploring Expedition to the Pacific Ocean and South Seas, the campaign document of Symmes's own former lecture partner, who has dropped the hollow Earth and kept the poles. Poe reads it the way a man reads something he intends to use. The same month he leaves the Messenger, claiming to have carried its circulation from seven hundred to three thousand five hundred. In February the second installment of Arthur Gordon Pym runs in its pages.
suggested_refs: Reynolds's 1836 Address to Congress, reviewed by Poe in the Southern Literary Messenger, January 1837

stops.name: New York, Harper and Brothers issue Pym
stops.date_confidence: July 1838 attested in the eapoe.org chronology; day not given, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: Harper and Brothers publish The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, the only novel he will finish: a stowaway in a coffin-sized crate, a mutiny, a wreck, cannibalism decided by lots, and a black island called Tsalal where the water runs in separable veins and the people recoil from anything white. Roughly seven hundred words of the sealing-voyage material are lifted straight out of Reynolds's Address into Chapter Sixteen. It is issued as a true account, with a preface signed by Pym himself explaining away Mr. Poe.
suggested_refs: The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket (New York: Harper & Brothers, July 1838)
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket'

stops.name: The Antarctic verge, the shrouded white figure
stops.date_confidence: not a dated event: a composite pin for the fictional latitude of Pym's last chapters and for the Antarctic verge the United States Exploring Expedition sailed to chart in the same year. The interlock pool dates the Wilkes pin 1838-01-01
stops.campa: South of the eighty-fourth parallel the sea turns warm and milky, white ash falls, the current quickens, and a cataract of vapor opens across the whole southern horizon. A shrouded human figure, larger than any dweller among men, the skin of it the perfect whiteness of snow, rises in the path of the boat, and the book stops in the middle of a sentence. Symmes's warm polar sea and open verge are the engine of the scene. The same year, in the same water, the United States Exploring Expedition sails under Wilkes to chart the actual ice.
suggested_refs: The final chapters of Pym and the 1838-1842 Wilkes Expedition charts of the Antarctic coast
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket'

stops.name: Philadelphia, Burton's and the Grotesque and Arabesque
stops.date_confidence: June 1839 attested for the Burton's appointment; day not given, defaulted to the first. The 1838 relocation and the five Philadelphia addresses are carried in the campa
stops.campa: The household moved to Philadelphia in 1838 and will keep five separate addresses inside the city before 1844, ending in the small brick house on North Seventh with its garden. In June 1839 William Burton takes him on at Burton's Gentleman's Magazine. Inside a year he prints The Fall of the House of Usher and William Wilson, whose schoolmaster carries the name of the clergyman at Stoke Newington, and Lea and Blanchard bring out Tales of the Grotesque and Arabesque in two volumes, twenty-five stories, the author paid in copies.
suggested_refs: Tales of the Grotesque and Arabesque, 2 vols. (Philadelphia: Lea & Blanchard, 1839)

stops.name: Philadelphia, the prospectus of The Penn
stops.date_confidence: June 1840 attested for the prospectus; day not given, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: In June he prints a prospectus for a magazine of his own, The Penn, to be edited by nobody but himself and to review American books without reference to who publishes them. Illness and a partner's collapse kill it before a first number exists. He renames it The Stylus and carries the prospectus for the rest of his life, resetting the type each time the plan moves and writing to men in three cities about capital. No issue of it is ever printed. It is the thing he wants most and the only one he never gets any part of.
suggested_refs: The 1840 prospectus of The Penn Magazine and its successor prospectuses for The Stylus

stops.name: Philadelphia, Graham's and the blood at the piano
stops.date_confidence: the Graham's appointment is dated 1841 in the pool without a month, defaulted to January; Virginia's hemorrhage is attested to January 1842 and is carried in the campa
stops.campa: George Graham takes over Burton's list and Poe with it, and at Graham's Magazine he publishes The Murders in the Rue Morgue and invents the detective story: a locked room, a bafflement, and a reasoner named C. Auguste Dupin who solves it from a chair. One of the witnesses is a laundress called Dubourg. In January 1842 Virginia is singing at the piano when a blood vessel bursts in her throat. She is twenty. The five years that follow run in a cycle of hemorrhage, recovery and hemorrhage, and he can do nothing about any of it.
suggested_refs: 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue,' Graham's Magazine, April 1841

stops.name: Philadelphia, the appointment not kept
stops.date_confidence: September 1842 attested; day not given, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: A place in the Philadelphia Custom House would pay a steady salary and leave the evenings free, and friends arrange the meeting. Poe does not appear. The report is that he was drinking, which is the report attached to most of the doors that close in these years. How much of it is illness, how much grief, and how much a constitution that could not take a single glass, the record does not settle and this file will not pretend to. The appointment goes elsewhere, Graham's is behind him within months, and the household is on nothing again.
suggested_refs: The Philadelphia Custom House appointment of 1842, missed

segments.name: The Raven and the Cottage at Fordham

stops.name: Berlin, Kosmos, volume the first
stops.date_confidence: inherited from humboldt.journey.json, which dates the first volume 1845-01-01; month and day there are conventional
stops.campa: At seventy-five, in Berlin, Alexander von Humboldt publishes the first volume of Kosmos, an attempt at the physical description of the universe taken as one connected whole. It sells out in months and is translated across Europe. Three years later a bankrupt American magazine writer will stand up in a New York lecture room, deliver his own account of the origin and the end of all matter, and dedicate the printed version to Humboldt, who had met the hollow-earth broadside from Missouri with silence twenty-seven years before.
suggested_refs: Kosmos, vol. 1 (Stuttgart and Tubingen, 1845), the book Eureka is dedicated toward

stops.name: New York, the Raven and nine dollars
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He has been in New York since 1844, first at the Evening Mirror, then at the Broadway Journal, which he edits and briefly owns. On the twenty-ninth of January the Mirror runs The Raven, and The American Review prints it under the name Quarles. He is paid nine dollars for it. Within weeks it is reprinted, parodied, set to music and recited across the country, and he is the most famous living writer in America, taken up by the literary parlors of the city and still living on what a magazine pays a hired hand.
suggested_refs: The Evening Mirror of 29 January 1845, first printing of 'The Raven'

stops.name: Fordham, the cottage in the country
stops.date_confidence: the move is dated 1846 in the pool without a month; defaulted to January
stops.campa: The Broadway Journal fails and takes his last position down with it. The household goes north out of the city to a white wooden cottage at Fordham, thirteen miles up, among rock and orchard, with the Harlem railroad below and a view toward the Sound. Virginia is dying in a room off the kitchen without enough bedding. Visitors describe a tortoiseshell cat lying on her chest for warmth and Poe's old army greatcoat spread over the straw. He is thirty-seven and out of the trade that fed him.
suggested_refs: The Poe Cottage at Fordham, now in the Bronx, preserved as a museum

stops.name: Fordham, Virginia dies in January
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of January Virginia Poe dies at the Fordham cottage of the tuberculosis that announced itself at a piano five years earlier. She is twenty-four, the age his mother was. He has now watched the same disease take his mother, his foster mother and his wife, and drink take his brother. No likeness of her alive exists; a watercolor is made after death and that is all there is. He collapses into a year of illness with Maria Clemm nursing him, and writes almost nothing for months.
suggested_refs: The posthumous watercolor portrait of Virginia Clemm Poe, the only known likeness

stops.name: New York, Eureka
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In February he lectures on the universe at the Society Library, and in July Putnam prints Eureka: A Prose Poem, dedicated to Alexander von Humboldt. It proposes an original unity, a single primordial particle diffused into matter by an act of divine volition, and a universe obliged to collapse back into that unity and begin again. He calls it a book of truths and asks that it be judged as a poem. Reviewers divide between brilliant and pantheistic. He says it will settle everything; in his lifetime it settles nothing.
suggested_refs: Eureka: A Prose Poem (New York: Geo. P. Putnam, 1848), dedicated to Alexander von Humboldt

stops.name: Providence, Sarah Helen Whitman
stops.date_confidence: the pool dates the Whitman courtship 1848 without a month; the courtship belongs to the autumn, and September is a reconstruction
stops.campa: The widower courts the poet Sarah Helen Whitman of Providence, six years older than he is, a Transcendentalist who wears mourning and who wrote about him before she met him. He proposes to her in a cemetery. Her mother ties up the property against him, her friends send warnings by post, and Poe swears abstinence as a condition of the engagement. In December it breaks over a report that he has broken the oath. He is thirty-nine and writing love letters in three states, trying to assemble a household out of pieces.
suggested_refs: Sarah Helen Whitman's Edgar Poe and His Critics (1860), her later defense of him

stops.name: Richmond, the widow Shelton
stops.date_confidence: year attested only; the Richmond courtship belongs to the summer of 1849, and the month is defaulted to January by the file convention rather than by any source
stops.campa: He comes back to Richmond and finds Sarah Elmira Royster again, the girl whose letters were intercepted twenty-three years ago, now the widowed Mrs. Shelton with property and children of her own. She agrees to him, conditionally. He joins the Sons of Temperance in the city and takes the pledge in public. He lectures on the poetic principle to full rooms in the town that raised him and is, by every account of that summer, well and working. On the twenty-seventh of September he takes the boat north.
suggested_refs: The Shelton house on Church Hill, Richmond, where Poe called in the summer of 1849

stops.name: Baltimore, found in another man's clothes
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He is found on the third of October outside a tavern on East Lombard Street that is serving as a ward polling place on an election day, semiconscious, unable to give an account of himself, and wearing clothes that are not his: a cheap ill-fitting suit and a palm-leaf hat where he had left Richmond in black. A note goes to a doctor who knows him. A carriage carries him to the Washington Medical College. Where he was between the twenty-eighth of September and that afternoon has never been established.
suggested_refs: Ryan's Fourth Ward polls, East Lombard Street, Baltimore, 3 October 1849

stops.name: Baltimore, the Washington Medical College
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death; the coordinates place the hospital at Broadway and Fayette rather than at the Baltimore city centroid the pool gives
stops.campa: He is put in a room in the hospital at Broadway and Fayette and never becomes able to account for himself. He is by turns delirious and quiet, and calls out through one night for a man named Reynolds. He dies at about five in the morning on the seventh of October, forty years old. The attending physician reports his last words afterward, and reports them differently again in later years. No death certificate survives, no autopsy was performed, and the cause has been argued over for the better part of two centuries.
stops.quote_source: reported by the attending physician at Washington Medical College, Baltimore, 7 October 1849
suggested_refs: Washington College Hospital at Broadway and Fayette, east Baltimore, since demolished

stops.name: Baltimore, the Western Burying Ground
stops.date_confidence: the pool gives October 1849 without a day; the burial followed immediately on the 7 October death and the day here is a reconstruction
stops.campa: A handful of mourners follow the coffin into the old Western Burying Ground of Baltimore's First Presbyterian Church. The service is short. He is laid in the family plot in the southeastern corner, plot twenty-seven, beside his grandfather David Poe Sr. and near his brother Henry, and the grave is left without a stone. A marker his cousin Neilson Poe orders is smashed in the marble yard by a derailed train before it can be set. The grave stays effectively anonymous for twenty-six years.
suggested_refs: Plot 27, the Poe family plot, Westminster Hall and Burying Ground, Baltimore

segments.name: The Slander, the Translator, and the Globe Over the Grave

stops.name: New York, Ludwig writes the obituary
stops.date_confidence: the pool dates the Griswold sequence 1849-1850 without days; the obituary appeared within days of the death and the day given here is a reconstruction
stops.campa: Two days after the death the New York Tribune prints an obituary signed Ludwig which announces that Poe is dead and adds that few will be much grieved by it. The writer is Rufus Wilmot Griswold, whom Poe had named his literary executor. Griswold follows it with a three-volume edition and a Memoir carrying letters he has forged and vices he has invented, and for twenty years that is the Poe the public is given, though Sarah Helen Whitman and George Rex Graham call it a lie in print at the time.
suggested_refs: The 'Ludwig' obituary, New York Tribune, October 1849, and Griswold's 1850 'Memoir of the Author'

stops.name: Paris, Baudelaire's eighteen years
stops.date_confidence: the pool gives the span 1847-1865 for the translations; this stop is dated to Histoires extraordinaires, 1856, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Charles Baudelaire reads a handful of translated tales in 1847 and says afterward that he found in them sentences he had thought of himself. He spends eighteen years turning Poe into French: Histoires extraordinaires in 1856, Nouvelles histoires extraordinaires in 1857, Histoires grotesques et serieuses in 1865, with Eureka and Arthur Gordon Pym besides. The versions become the definitive ones. Continental Europe is handed a Poe of greater stature than America has yet granted him, by a poet who treats the work as a personal rescue.
suggested_refs: Baudelaire's Histoires extraordinaires (Paris: Michel Levy, 1856) and its preface on Poe

stops.name: Baltimore, pennies for Poe
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In October 1865 the public schoolteachers of Baltimore open a subscription and the children bring in pennies. By March 1871 the fund holds about five hundred and eighty-seven dollars, which is not enough. George W. Childs of Philadelphia gives six hundred and fifty more. Hugh Sisson, the marble king of Baltimore, cuts the monument and Adalbert Volck models the portrait medallion. On the seventeenth of November 1875 the remains are moved to the corner of Greene and Fayette and the stone is dedicated, John H. B. Latrobe speaking.
suggested_refs: The Poe monument at Greene and Fayette, dedicated 17 November 1875

stops.name: Baltimore, the Toaster at the first stone
stops.date_confidence: the widely repeated 1949 start date is a fabrication: Sam Porpora admitted falsely telling a reporter the visits began that year, and in 2007 he claimed instead to have invented the tradition in the 1960s, a decade after the first newspaper report. Wikipedia traces the visits to sometime in the 1930s, first printed in the Baltimore Evening Sun in 1950. The year here is a floor, not a date
stops.campa: Some time in the 1930s a figure in black with a white scarf begins arriving at the original grave marker before dawn on the nineteenth of January, leaving three roses and a half bottle of cognac, and going. The first newspaper account of him appears in 1950. He comes every birthday for decades and the visits pass at some point to a younger man. On the nineteenth of January 2009, the two hundredth birthday, he comes for the last time. Nobody ever stopped him, questioned him, or established who either of them was.
suggested_refs: The Baltimore Evening Sun report of 1950, the earliest printed notice of the Poe Toaster

stops.name: San Isidro, Villa Ocampo: the grandfather of the genre
stops.date_confidence: inherited from borges.journey.json, which dates the Bioy meeting 1932-01-01 as traditional; the Borges statements about Poe are lifelong and not tied to this date
stops.campa: At a lunch in Victoria Ocampo's house at San Isidro, Jorge Luis Borges meets Adolfo Bioy Casares, and out of that afternoon come four decades of joint detective stories, a shared pseudonym and an anthology of the fantastic. Borges will say from lecture platforms and in essays that the detective story was invented by one man in one story, that Poe made the genre and made its reader, and that anyone reading detective fiction anywhere is a reader Poe invented. The Rue Morgue reaches the Rio de la Plata and is naturalized there.
suggested_refs: Borges and Bioy Casares, Los mejores cuentos policiales, and Borges's lectures on Poe

stops.name: Paris, Marie Bonaparte reads the tales
stops.date_confidence: 1933 attested for the publication; month and day not given, defaulted to January. The coordinates are inherited from the Paris stop of freud.journey.json
stops.campa: Princess Marie Bonaparte, Freud's analysand and the woman whose money and diplomacy will get the Freud family out of Vienna, publishes a study of Poe running close to a thousand pages and reading the whole body of tales through the dead mother of 1811. Freud writes a foreword to it. It becomes the founding document of psychoanalytic literary criticism and, for decades, the most influential book anyone has written about Poe. Five years later the Freuds break their escape at her house in this city, bound for London.
suggested_refs: Marie Bonaparte, Edgar Poe: etude psychanalytique (Paris, 1933), with Freud's foreword

stops.name: Boston, Poe returns to the city that let him go
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinates are the Boylston and Charles Street corner rather than the Bay Village point given in the pool
stops.campa: At the corner of Boylston and Charles, at the edge of the Common and a short walk from the ground where the house he was born in stood, a life-sized bronze Poe strides north into the wind with a raven flying out ahead of him and a suitcase burst open behind, its papers spilling in bronze along the sidewalk. Stefanie Rocknak made it. It is unveiled on the fifth of October 2014 with Robert Pinsky in attendance. He is walking away from the harbor where he enlisted under a false name, back into the city.
suggested_refs: Stefanie Rocknak, 'Poe Returning to Boston' (2014), Edgar Allan Poe Square, Boston
